correctness.rationale: Write the monic polynomial with the five distinct column roots; at a root, z^5 equals (sum of the roots) times z^4 plus a combination of powers 0 through 3. Thus the determinant is Vandermonde times that sum and the first four rows give rank at least four. The frozen conductor reduction is sound: for a prime-power part p^a of the normalized ratio conductor, the p^a cyclotomic polynomial stays irreducible over the prime-to-p field by the product degree. Its coefficient constraints make each residue block modulo p^(a-1) a zero subsum. Only one such block can occur by minimality, so all ratios have p-part at most p. At a=1, all p residues must appear: if any residue is absent all block coefficients vanish, minimality forces a single occupied residue, and p would then be absent from the ratio conductor. Hence p<=5 and the conductor divides 30. An independent tensor-basis check of all size-2 through size-5 subsets of the 30th roots found 15, 10, 0 and 6 minimal sets, respectively, with the six minimal five-sets exactly the pentagons. Alternatively, in the conductor argument a minimal five-set with factor 5 must have one term in each residue, with equal prime-to-5 factors by coefficient equality; without factor 5 its conductor divides 6, where an opposite-free set has size at most three. The only nonminimal five-term partition has component sizes 2 and 3. For each antipodal pair the two endpoints lie in distinct cosets of the subgroup of size three, leaving N/3-2 available triples; the opposite pair in the union is unique since an endpoint's antipode is already in the pair and a triangle has no antipodes. This proves the all-N count and the full-spark boundary including N=6. Scope: N>=6, unordered distinct columns and precisely the specified five rows; no general pattern or smaller-minor theorem follows from the finite replay alone.

evidence: Theorem 4.8 and the coset definition leave only one order-five coset or a disjoint order-two and order-three coset. There are N/5 cosets of order five if 5 divides N. When 6 divides N each of N/2 order-two cosets intersects exactly two of the N/3 order-three cosets because the two subgroups intersect trivially. Counting the others gives (N/2)(N/3-2); no duplicate union can contain two distinct antipodal pairs. The two cases are disjoint because pentagons have no antipodes.
